To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
antenatal maternal depression/anxiety is a risk factor for the neurobehaviour of the child.

antenatal maternal depression, anxiety, and stress are linked to neurobehavioural problems in the offspring and that this link is independent of the effects of post natal maternal depression, and anxiety.

antenatal maternal psychological distress (stress and anxiety) is associated with neurodevelopmental problems in the child, and that the association persists even after controlling for postnatal maternal psychological distress.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of maternal anxiety and stress during pregnancy on the development of the fetus/child.
the long-term effects of maternal stress and anxiety during pregnancy on the child's cognitive, behavioural and emotional development.
the long-term effects of antenatally induced stress on the child.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no conclusive evidence that antenatal stress/anxiety is related to neurobehavioral outcomes in the child.
the evidence is strong and consistent that there are adverse long term effects of maternal anxiety/stress during pregnancy on the neurobehaviour of the fetus/child.

there is a link between antepartum maternal anxiety/stress (and to a lesser degree depression) and neurobehavioral development in the offspring, but that the mechanisms underlying this association are not fully known.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fetus is not a passive receiver, but a dynamic, active, responsive, and developing organism.
antenatal stress is associated with adverse neurobehavioral outcomes for the child, and that this association is independent of postnatal factors.
antenatal maternal psychological distress has a direct and indirect effect on the fetus and newborn, and that this effect may persist into childhood and adolescence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the fetus is not just a passive passenger, but a very active participant in the development of the brain and other organs, and in the regulation of the maternal physiology and behaviour.
antenatal maternal distress can affect the fetus and child in a number of ways.
maternal anxiety during pregnancy is associated with increased risk for a range of adverse outcomes in the offspring.
